rows.query: What were Berkshire's total operating earnings and operating earnings per share in 1977?
rows.answer:
Operating earnings in 1977 of $21,904,000, or $22.54 per share, were moderately better than anticipated a year ago. [1]

Of these earnings, $1.43 per share resulted from substantial realized capital gains by Blue Chip Stamps which, to the extent of our proportional interest in that company, are included in our operating earnings figure. [1]

Capital gains or losses realized directly by Berkshire Hathaway Inc. or its insurance subsidiaries are not included in our calculation of operating earnings. [1]

In 1977 our operating earnings on beginning equity capital amounted to 19%, slightly better than last year and above both our own long-term average and that of American industry in aggregate. [2]

But, while our operating earnings per share were up 37% from the year before, our beginning capital was up 24%, making the gain in earnings per share considerably less impressive than it might appear at first glance. [2]

Nevertheless, we expect a reasonably good year and our present estimate, subject to the usual caveats regarding the frailties of forecasts, is that operating earnings will improve somewhat on a per share basis during 1978. [4]

rows.query: What warning did Buffett give in 1982 about paying too high a purchase price for an excellent company's stock?
rows.answer:
The market, like the Lord, helps those who help themselves. [1]

But, unlike the Lord, the market does not forgive those who know not what they do. [1]

For the investor, a too-high purchase price for the stock of an excellent company can undo the effects of a subsequent decade of favorable business developments. [1]

Should the stock market advance to considerably higher levels, our ability to utilize capital effectively in partialownership positions will be reduced or eliminated. [1]

While high stock prices in the future would make our performance look good temporarily, they would hurt our long-term business prospects rather than help them. [3]

Our willingness to purchase either partial or total ownership positions in favorably-situated businesses, coupled with reasonable discipline about the prices we are willing to pay, should give us a good chance of achieving our goal. [4]

rows.query: By 1983, what combination of enduring Goodwill and tangible assets had Buffett come to prefer in businesses?
rows.answer:
For years the traditional wisdom – long on tradition, short on wisdom – held that inflation protection was best provided by businesses laden with natural resources, plants and machinery, or other tangible assets ("In Goods We Trust"). [1]

Asset-heavy businesses generally earn low rates of return – rates that often barely provide enough capital to fund the inflationary needs of the existing business, with nothing left over for real growth, for distribution to owners, or for acquisition of new businesses. [1]

Keynes identified my problem: “The difficulty lies not in the new ideas but in escaping from the old ones.” My escape was long delayed, in part because most of what I had been taught by the same teacher had been (and continues to be) so extraordinarily valuable. [2]

Ultimately, business experience, direct and vicarious, produced my present strong preference for businesses that possess large amounts of enduring Goodwill and that utilize a minimum of tangible assets. [2]

I recommend the Appendix to those who are comfortable with accounting terminology and who have an interest in understanding the business aspects of Goodwill. [2]

My own thinking has changed drastically from 35 years ago when I was taught to favor tangible assets and to shun businesses whose value depended largely upon economic Goodwill. [8]

rows.query: According to the 1995 letter, what method of selling gave GEICO an enormous cost advantage over competitors selling through agents?
rows.answer:
Though my only credentials were that I was a student of Graham's, "Davy" graciously spent four hours or so showering me with both kindness and instruction. [1]

No one has ever received a better half-day course in how the insurance industry functions nor in the factors that enable one company to excel over others. [1]

As Davy made clear, GEICO's method of selling - direct marketing - gave it an enormous cost advantage over competitors that sold through agents, a form of distribution so ingrained in the business of these insurers that it was impossible for them to give it up. [1]

After my session with Davy, I was more excited about GEICO than I have ever been about a stock. [1]

But in the next 20 years, the GEICO stock I sold grew in value to about $1.3 million, which taught me a lesson about the inadvisability of selling a stake in an identifiably-wonderful company. [3]

In any event, I accumulated 350 shares of GEICO during the year, at a cost of $10,282. [6]
